name: North American Racer
habitat: Fields, meadows, open woodland, brushy edges, dunes and suburbs
range: Most of the USA and southern Canada (Ontario, British Columbia and the prairies), except the driest south-west; into Mexico and Central America
diet: Insects, frogs, lizards, rodents, birds and other snakes
ids: Long, slim and very fast, often holding its head high as it hunts.
Adults are plain: black in the east, blue-grey in the Midwest, olive, brown or grey in the west, with a paler chin and throat.
Large eyes and smooth, satiny scales.
Young are grey with a row of red-brown blotches, quite unlike the adults, and change colour in their second year.

look.colour: Black, blue-grey, olive, brown or grey; chin white or yellow
look.head: Rounded, with big eyes

fact: Despite the scientific name it does not constrict; it simply overpowers prey and swallows it alive.

name: Coachwhip
habitat: Open sandy country: sandhills, pine scrub, prairie, desert grassland and old fields
range: Southern USA from North Carolina and Florida west to Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas and New Mexico; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, snakes, rodents, birds and large insects
active: By day, even in the heat
ids: Extremely long and slender, with a long, thin tail.
In the east the front of the body is dark brown or black, fading to tan or reddish towards the tail.
The tail scales look braided, like the plaited leather of a whip.
Large eyes, smooth scales and a narrow head; it races off at the slightest disturbance.

look.colour: Dark brown to black in front, tan or reddish behind
look.head: Narrow, with big eyes

fact: Old stories say a coachwhip chases people and whips them with its tail; it does neither.

name: Red Coachwhip
habitat: Desert scrub, grassland, chaparral and open rocky hillsides
range: The south-west: California, Arizona, Nevada, Utah and New Mexico; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, snakes, rodents and birds
ids: Very long and slender, often pink, red or tan, sometimes black in southern Arizona.
Wide dark crossbars on the neck in many snakes, fading down the body.
Braided-looking tail scales, large eyes and a narrow head.
fact: It hunts with its head raised above the plants, watching for lizards to move.

name: California Striped Racer
habitat: Chaparral, coastal sage scrub, oak woodland and rocky hillsides
range: California, mainly west of the deserts; into Baja California
diet: Lizards, frogs, snakes, rodents and insects
ids: Black or dark brown, with a single cream, yellow or orange stripe along each side.
Slim and fast, with large eyes.
The throat and belly are pale, often pinkish under the tail.

look.colour: Black or dark brown with a pale yellow stripe on each side
look.head: Narrow, with big eyes

fact: The Alameda Striped Racer, a form with orange stripes from the San Francisco Bay area, is a threatened species.

name: Striped Whipsnake
habitat: Sagebrush, desert grassland, canyons and juniper woodland
range: The Great Basin and south-west: Washington, Oregon, Idaho, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and west Texas; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, snakes, rodents and birds
ids: Slim and fast, dark grey, black or olive on the back.
A cream stripe along each side, split lengthwise by a thin dark line.
Large eyes; the belly turns yellow then pink towards the tail.

look.colour: Dark grey or olive with cream stripes
look.pattern: Pale side stripes split by a dark line
look.head: Narrow, with big eyes

fact: It often climbs into bushes to hunt and to bask.

name: Sonoran Whipsnake
habitat: Rocky desert foothills, canyons, oak woodland and thornscrub
range: Arizona and south-western New Mexico; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, frogs, birds and their eggs
ids: Olive, grey or bluish, with two or three pale stripes on each side of the front half of the body.
The stripes fade towards the tail.
Very slim with large eyes; often climbs into bushes and trees.

look.pattern: Pale side stripes on the front half
look.head: Narrow, with big eyes

fact: It hunts birds in the branches of desert trees.

name: Schott's Whipsnake
habitat: Thornscrub, brushland and grassland
range: South and west Texas; into north-eastern Mexico
diet: Lizards, snakes and rodents
ids: Grey-green to bluish, with two pale stripes along each side.
Often reddish or orange on the sides of the neck.
Slim and fast with large eyes.
fact: The Ruthven's Whipsnake of the Rio Grande valley is now treated as part of this species.

name: Baja California Coachwhip
habitat: Desert scrub, rocky hillsides and coastal scrub
range: Far southern California near the Mexican border; mainly Baja California
diet: Lizards, snakes and rodents
ids: A coachwhip that is either dark grey-brown with pale crossbars or pale yellowish with dark bars on the neck.
Long, slender and fast, with large eyes.
fact: In the USA it is found only in a small corner of San Diego County.

name: Western Patch-nosed Snake
habitat: Desert scrub, chaparral, sandy flats and rocky canyons
range: California, Nevada, Utah and Arizona; into Mexico
diet: Lizards and their eggs, and small snakes
ids: A thick, flap-like scale curves over the tip of the snout, like a patch.
A broad pale stripe down the middle of the back, bordered by dark brown stripes.
Slim and fast.

look.colour: Grey-brown with a cream or yellow back stripe
look.pattern: Pale back stripe between dark stripes
look.head: With a patch-like scale on the snout

fact: It uses the enlarged snout scale to dig up buried lizard eggs.

name: Texas Patch-nosed Snake
habitat: Brushland, rocky hills, grassland and woodland edges
range: Texas and southern Oklahoma; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, their eggs and small rodents
ids: A pale orange or tan stripe down the middle of the back, bordered by broad dark stripes.
A raised patch-like scale on the snout.
Slim and fast.

look.colour: Brown with an orange or tan back stripe
look.pattern: Pale back stripe between dark stripes
look.head: With a patch-like snout scale

fact: It was split from the Mountain Patch-nosed Snake in 2016.

name: Mountain Patch-nosed Snake
habitat: Rocky canyons, oak and pine woodland in mountains
range: Arizona, New Mexico and west Texas; into Mexico
diet: Lizards and their eggs
ids: A cream or pale grey stripe down the back between two dark stripes.
A raised scale over the snout.
Slim, smooth and quick.

look.colour: Grey-brown with a pale back stripe
look.pattern: Pale back stripe between dark stripes
look.head: With a patch-like snout scale

fact: It lives higher in the mountains than its desert relatives.

name: Big Bend Patch-nosed Snake
habitat: Desert flats, rocky foothills and creosote scrub
range: Arizona, New Mexico and west Texas; into Mexico
diet: Lizards and their eggs
ids: A pale orange or tan back stripe with thin dark stripes on each side.
A large, flap-like scale on the snout.
Slim and fast.

look.colour: Tan or grey with an orange-tinged back stripe
look.pattern: Pale back stripe with thin dark borders
look.head: With a patch-like snout scale

fact: It is a snake of the Chihuahuan and Sonoran Deserts, active even at midday.

name: Speckled Racer
habitat: Thornscrub and dense woodland near water
range: The far south of Texas (the lower Rio Grande valley); through Mexico to South America
diet: Frogs and toads
ids: Black, with a yellow or green spot in the middle of nearly every scale, giving a speckled look.
A dark stripe behind the eye.
Slim and fast, with large eyes.

look.pattern: Speckled: one pale spot per scale
look.head: With big eyes and a dark eye stripe

fact: In the USA it lives only in the last patches of thornscrub along the lower Rio Grande.

name: Rough Greensnake
habitat: Shrubs, vines and trees along lake shores, streams and woodland edges
range: South-eastern and central USA, from New Jersey and Florida west to Kansas and Texas
diet: Caterpillars, crickets, spiders and other insects
active: By day; sleeps coiled in branches at night
ids: Bright, plain green above and yellow or cream below.
Very slender, with a long tail; spends most of its time in shrubs and vines.
Its scales are keeled (ridged), unlike the Smooth Greensnake's.
Large eyes and a narrow head.

look.colour: Bright green above, yellow or cream below
look.head: Narrow, with big eyes
look.body: Very slender, with a long tail

fact: It sways like a vine in the breeze, which makes it very hard to spot among leaves.

name: Smooth Greensnake
habitat: Meadows, prairie, open grassy woodland and marsh edges
range: Southern Canada (Nova Scotia to Saskatchewan) and the northern USA, south along the Appalachians; isolated groups in the west
diet: Caterpillars, crickets, grasshoppers and spiders
ids: Small and bright plain green, with a white or pale yellow belly.
Smooth, unridged scales.
Lives on the ground in grass rather than in bushes.
fact: After it dies its green colour fades to blue, because the yellow pigment breaks down first.

name: Central American Indigo Snake
habitat: Thornscrub, brushland, riverside woods and coastal plains
range: South Texas; through Mexico and Central America
diet: Snakes (including rattlesnakes), lizards, frogs, rodents and birds
ids: A huge, glossy snake, brownish or olive at the front shading to black on the rear and tail.
Dark diagonal "tear marks" run down from the eye across the lips.
Smooth, shiny scales and a large head.

look.colour: Brownish in front, glossy black behind
look.pattern: Plain, with dark marks below the eye
look.head: Large, with dark tear-like streaks

fact: It eats rattlesnakes and is largely resistant to their venom.

name: Eastern Indigo Snake
habitat: Longleaf pine sandhills with gopher tortoise burrows, flatwoods, hammocks and wetland edges
range: Florida and south-eastern Georgia; a few reintroduced in Alabama
diet: Snakes (including venomous ones), frogs, small mammals and birds
ids: The longest native snake in the USA: glossy blue-black all over.
The chin and throat are often reddish or orange-brown.
Smooth scales with a blue sheen in sunlight.
fact: It is a threatened species that depends on gopher tortoise burrows for winter shelter.

name: Eastern Ratsnake
habitat: Forests, farmland, barns, suburbs and rocky hillsides; a superb climber
range: Eastern USA from Vermont and New York to Georgia, west to the Mississippi; southern Ontario
diet: Rats, mice, squirrels, birds and their eggs
active: By day in spring and autumn, at night in summer
ids: A long, powerful climber; adults are usually shiny black, with traces of a blotched pattern showing between the scales.
The chin and throat are white, and the belly has black and white checks near the head.
In cross-section the body is shaped like a loaf of bread, with corners on the belly edges that help it climb bark.
Young snakes are pale grey with dark grey blotches.

look.pattern: Faint blotches; plain in old adults
look.head: Squarish, a little wider than the neck
look.body: Long and muscular, with a flat belly

fact: When threatened it freezes in a series of kinks and may vibrate its tail in dry leaves.

name: Western Ratsnake
habitat: Forests, rocky hills, river woods, farmland and towns
range: West of the Mississippi: Missouri, Arkansas, Louisiana, Iowa, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas
diet: Rodents, birds and their eggs
ids: In the north, black with a faint blotched pattern; in Texas, yellowish or grey-brown with dark brown blotches.
Texas snakes often show reddish or orange skin between the scales and a grey head.
A long, strong climber with a white or grey chin.
Young are grey with dark blotches.

look.colour: Black, or yellow-grey with dark blotches
look.pattern: Dark blotches, faint in black adults
look.head: Squarish and grey or black

fact: Texas Ratsnakes are notorious raiders of chicken coops and bird nests.

name: Yellow Ratsnake
habitat: Pine woods, hammocks, swamps, farmland and suburbs of the coastal plain
range: The south-eastern coastal plain, from Virginia and North Carolina to Florida and the Gulf coast
diet: Rodents, birds and their eggs, and frogs
ids: Yellow, orange or olive with four dark stripes running along the body.
In the north of its range many are darker or blackish with faint stripes.
A long climber with a squarish body and a pale, unmarked chin.
Young are grey with dark blotches.
fact: The orange "Everglades" form of south Florida is the most colourful ratsnake in North America.

name: Red Cornsnake
habitat: Pine woods, overgrown fields, farmland, rocky hillsides and suburbs
range: South-eastern USA, from New Jersey to Florida, west to Louisiana and Kentucky
diet: Mice, rats, birds and lizards
active: At dusk and night; also by day in spring
ids: Orange, red or brownish saddle-shaped blotches outlined in black on a paler orange or grey body.
A spear-point mark on top of the head reaching between the eyes.
A bold black-and-white checkerboard belly, like Indian corn.
Round pupils and smooth to weakly ridged scales.

look.head: With a spear-point mark on top

fact: It is the world's most popular pet snake, and is often killed in the wild by people who mistake it for a copperhead.

name: Great Plains Ratsnake
habitat: Rocky hillsides, prairie, canyons, farmland and riverside woods
range: The plains and south-west: Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, Missouri, Colorado and New Mexico; into Mexico
diet: Rodents, bats, birds and lizards
ids: Grey or tan with dark grey-brown, dark-edged blotches down the back.
A spear-point mark on top of the head, like the cornsnake's.
A grey-and-white checkered belly.

look.colour: Grey or tan with brown blotches
look.head: With a spear-point mark on top

fact: It is a western relative of the cornsnake, with muted greys instead of reds.

name: Slowinski's Cornsnake
habitat: Pine and hardwood forests, often on sandy soil
range: Western Louisiana, eastern Texas and southern Arkansas
diet: Rodents, birds and lizards
ids: Like a cornsnake but browner: brown-red blotches on a grey-brown body.
A spear-point mark on the head.
Checkered belly.

look.head: With a spear-point mark on top

fact: It is named after Joseph Slowinski, a herpetologist who died of a krait bite in Myanmar in 2001.

name: Eastern Foxsnake
habitat: Marshes, wet meadows, shorelines, farmland and woodland edges
range: Around the Great Lakes: southern Ontario, Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois and Wisconsin
diet: Mice, voles, birds and their eggs
ids: Yellowish to tan with large dark brown or black blotches down the back and smaller ones on the sides.
An unmarked orange-brown or reddish head, which leads people to mistake it for a copperhead.
A yellow belly checked with black.
When alarmed it vibrates its tail and gives off a musky smell.

look.colour: Yellow-tan with dark brown blotches; head orange-brown
look.head: Plain orange-brown, rather blunt

fact: Its name comes from its musk, said to smell like a fox; there are no copperheads in most of its range.

name: Western Foxsnake
habitat: Prairie, farmland, river valleys and woodland edges
range: The upper Midwest: Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, South Dakota, Wisconsin, Illinois and Missouri
diet: Mice, voles, birds and eggs
ids: Yellow-tan with large dark brown blotches.
A plain reddish or brown head.
A yellow belly checked with black.
fact: It and the Eastern Foxsnake look alike; the two were separated by their DNA and the Mississippi River.

name: Baird's Ratsnake
habitat: Rocky canyons, wooded hills and limestone country
range: West and central Texas; into north-eastern Mexico
diet: Rodents, bats and birds
ids: Orange-grey to yellowish, with four faint dark stripes along the body.
Each scale often looks orange at the base with a grey tip, giving a glowing look.
Young are grey with dark crossbars.
fact: It is a snake of the Edwards Plateau and the Big Bend, where it climbs cliffs and trees.

name: Trans-Pecos Ratsnake
habitat: Rocky desert, canyons and desert flats
range: West Texas and southern New Mexico; into Mexico
diet: Rodents, bats and birds
ids: Yellow or tan with dark brown H-shaped blotches down the back.
Very large, bulging eyes, with a row of small scales beneath each eye.
A plain, rounded head.
fact: It is almost never seen by day; road-cruising at night in the Big Bend is the classic way to find one.

name: Green Ratsnake
habitat: Wooded canyons and pine-oak forest in mountains
range: South-eastern Arizona and south-western New Mexico; through Mexico and Central America
diet: Rodents, birds and lizards
ids: Plain olive-green or greenish-grey above, with a pale yellowish belly.
Young are grey or tan with dark blotches.
A long, slim climber with a fairly narrow head.
fact: In the USA it lives only in a few mountain ranges near the Mexican border.

name: Gophersnake
habitat: Grassland, prairie, desert scrub, farmland, open woodland and chaparral
range: Western and central North America, from British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan to California, the Great Plains and Texas; into Mexico
diet: Gophers, ground squirrels, mice, rabbits, birds and eggs
active: By day; at night in hot weather
ids: A large, heavy snake, yellow, cream or tan with dark brown or black squarish blotches down the back.
A dark band across the head between the eyes, and a dark stripe from each eye to the jaw.
A narrow head with round pupils and a pointed tail without a rattle.
When threatened it hisses loudly, flattens its head and shakes its tail, imitating a rattlesnake.

look.pattern: Dark squarish blotches; smaller ones on the sides
look.head: Narrow, with a dark band between the eyes
look.body: Large and heavy, with keeled scales

fact: Its rattlesnake act is so convincing that many are killed by mistake; it is a valuable catcher of rodents.

name: Pinesnake
habitat: Sandy pine barrens, longleaf pine sandhills and dry oak woods
range: South-eastern USA: New Jersey, the Carolinas, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee and Kentucky
diet: Pocket gophers, moles, mice and eggs
active: By day; spends much time in burrows
ids: A large, powerful snake: in the north white or cream with black blotches, in Florida tan with brown blotches, and black in Mississippi.
A large, pointed snout scale used for digging.
Hisses loudly with a vibrating flap in the throat, and keeled scales.

look.colour: White, cream or tan with black or brown blotches; some all black
look.head: Small and pointed, made for digging

fact: Pinesnakes dig their own nest tunnels in sand, unusual among snakes.

name: Eastern Kingsnake
habitat: Pine woods, swamp edges, fields, farmland and stream banks
range: The eastern USA from New Jersey to north Florida and west to the Appalachians and Alabama
diet: Other snakes (including copperheads and rattlesnakes), lizards, rodents and turtle eggs
ids: Glossy black or dark brown with narrow white or yellow crossbands that join along the sides like a chain.
Smooth, shiny scales and a small, rounded head.
A black-and-white or yellow checkered belly.

look.colour: Glossy black with white or yellow chain links
look.head: Small and rounded

fact: Kingsnakes are immune to the venom of North American pit vipers and eat them.

name: Speckled Kingsnake
habitat: Prairies, swamp edges, river bottoms, farmland and suburbs
range: The central USA: the Mississippi valley from Iowa and Illinois to the Gulf coast, Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas
diet: Snakes, lizards, rodents, birds and eggs
ids: Black or dark brown, with a small yellow or white spot on almost every scale: a "salt and pepper" look.
Glossy, smooth scales and a rounded head.
Faint pale crossbands may show through the speckles.
fact: When grabbed it smears a smelly musk and pecks with a twisting body, but it rarely bites.

name: Black Kingsnake
habitat: Wooded hills, fields, stream banks and farmland
range: The Ohio and Tennessee valleys: Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Kentucky, Tennessee, Alabama and nearby states
diet: Snakes, lizards, rodents and eggs
ids: Mostly glossy black, with faint white or yellow specks or traces of thin chain bands.
A black-and-white or yellow checked belly.
Smooth, shiny scales and a rounded head.

look.pattern: Mostly plain, faint speckles or chain marks
look.head: Small and rounded

fact: Black Kingsnakes are often confused with black ratsnakes and racers, which have duller or ridged scales.

name: California Kingsnake
habitat: Almost anywhere: desert, chaparral, woodland, grassland, farmland and gardens
range: California, Oregon, Nevada, Utah and Arizona; into Mexico
diet: Snakes (including rattlesnakes), lizards, rodents, birds and eggs
active: By day; at night in summer
ids: Bold bands of white or cream on black or brown, the bands widening on the belly.
Some snakes are striped instead, with one pale stripe down the back.
Smooth, glossy scales and a rounded head.

look.colour: Black or brown with white or cream
look.head: Small and rounded

fact: Its black-and-white bands look strikingly like those of the deadly Asian kraits, though the two are unrelated.

name: Desert Kingsnake
habitat: Desert grassland, thornscrub, river valleys and farmland
range: Arizona, New Mexico and west Texas; into Mexico
diet: Snakes, lizards, rodents and eggs
ids: Dark brown or black, with yellow speckles on the sides.
Narrow yellow crossbars across the back.
Glossy, smooth scales.

look.colour: Black or brown with yellow speckles
look.head: Small and rounded

fact: It is the desert member of the common kingsnake group, between the Speckled and the California Kingsnake.

name: Eastern Milksnake
habitat: Woodland, fields, rocky hillsides, barns, old buildings and gardens
range: South-eastern Canada (Ontario, Quebec) and the north-eastern USA, south along the Appalachians and west to Minnesota
diet: Mice, voles, small snakes and lizards
active: Mostly at night; under boards and stones by day
ids: Grey or tan with large reddish-brown blotches edged in black down the back, and smaller ones on the sides.
Often a pale Y- or V-shaped mark on the back of the neck.
A black-and-white checkerboard belly.
Smooth, glossy scales and round pupils.

look.colour: Grey or tan with reddish-brown blotches
look.head: With a pale Y or V mark on the neck

fact: The old myth that it milks cows comes from finding it in barns, where it hunts mice.

name: Western Milksnake
habitat: Prairie, rocky hillsides, river valleys and open woodland
range: The Great Plains and south-west: Kansas, Nebraska, Colorado, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Utah and nearby states
diet: Lizards, small snakes and rodents
ids: Rings of red, black and white or yellow; the red rings touch the black, not the yellow.
A black snout and head, often with pale flecks.
Glossy, smooth scales.

look.colour: Red, black and white or yellow
look.head: Black, small and rounded

fact: Its coral-snake colours are a bluff: it is harmless, though few predators want to find out.

name: Mexican Milksnake
habitat: Thornscrub, grassland and river valleys
range: South and west Texas; into north-eastern Mexico
diet: Lizards, small snakes and rodents
ids: Very wide red rings bordered by black, separated by narrow yellow or white rings.
A black head and snout.
Glossy, smooth scales.

look.pattern: Wide red rings: red touches black
look.head: Black

fact: In Texas it shares its range with the Texas Coral Snake, where red touches yellow instead.

name: Scarlet Kingsnake
habitat: Pine flatwoods and hammocks, often under the bark of dead pines
range: South-eastern USA, from Virginia and Kentucky to Florida and west to the Mississippi
diet: Lizards (especially skinks), small snakes and eggs
active: At night; by day hides under bark and logs
ids: Small, with rings of red, black and yellow or white; red touches black.
A red snout (the coral snake's snout is black).
Glossy and slim.

look.colour: Red, black and yellow or white
look.head: Red snout

fact: Where coral snakes live, scarlet kingsnakes are most convincing mimics: same colours, different order.

name: Prairie Kingsnake
habitat: Prairie, old fields, farmland and open woodland
range: The central USA: from Maryland and Kentucky to Florida, and west to Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas
diet: Rodents, lizards, frogs and small snakes
active: By day and at night; often under cover
ids: Grey-brown or tan with small brown or reddish dark-edged blotches down the back.
Some old snakes fade to plain brown with faint stripes.
A small head and smooth, glossy scales.
fact: It is a secretive burrower and is most often seen crossing roads after spring rain.

name: Mole Kingsnake
habitat: Fields, pine woods and farmland on loose soil
range: The south-east: Maryland and Virginia to north Florida, west to Tennessee and Mississippi
diet: Moles, mice, lizards and small snakes
active: Mostly underground; seen at night and after rain
ids: Brown with small reddish-brown blotches edged in dark brown.
Small head and smooth, glossy scales.
Old snakes may darken and lose their pattern.
fact: It spends so much time underground that many people in its range never see one.

name: Sonoran Mountain Kingsnake
habitat: Rocky canyons, streams and pine-oak woodland in mountains
range: Arizona, Utah, Nevada and New Mexico; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, small snakes, rodents and nestling birds
active: By day in spring, at dusk in summer
ids: Rings of red, black and white; red touches black.
A white or pale snout.
Glossy and slim.
fact: It is a snake of the "sky island" mountains of the south-west.

name: Madrean Mountain Kingsnake
habitat: Pine-oak woodland and canyons in mountains
range: South-eastern Arizona and south-western New Mexico; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, small snakes and rodents
ids: Rings of red, black and white, with more black than its relatives; red touches black.
A pale snout.
Glossy and slim.
fact: It was split from the Sonoran Mountain Kingsnake in 2011.

name: California Mountain Kingsnake
habitat: Mountain forests of pine and oak, often near streams and rocky slopes
range: California, Oregon and southern Washington; into Baja California
diet: Lizards, small snakes, nestling birds and eggs
ids: Rings of red, black and white; red touches black.
A black snout.
The red rings are often split by black across the back.
fact: There are no coral snakes in California, yet it still copies their warning colours.

name: Coast Mountain Kingsnake
habitat: Coastal and mountain forests, chaparral and canyons
range: Coastal and southern California; into Baja California
diet: Lizards, small snakes, birds and eggs
ids: Rings of red, black and white; red touches black.
The snout is often red or flecked with red.
Glossy and slim.
fact: It was recognised as separate from the California Mountain Kingsnake in 2016.

name: Gray-banded Kingsnake
habitat: Rocky limestone canyons, cliffs and desert hills
range: West Texas and south-eastern New Mexico; into Mexico
diet: Lizards and their eggs, and small rodents
ids: Grey, with black crossbands; in many snakes the bands have orange-red centres.
Large eyes and a broad head.
Very variable from place to place.

look.colour: Grey with black and orange bands
look.pattern: Black crossbands, some with orange centres
look.head: Broad, with big eyes

fact: It was once so rarely seen that collectors searched rock cuts in the Big Bend night after night to find one.

name: Scarletsnake
habitat: Sandy pine woods, sandhills and fields
range: South-eastern USA from New Jersey to Florida, west to Louisiana and Oklahoma
diet: Reptile eggs, which it slits open with enlarged rear teeth
ids: Red blotches (saddles) edged in black on a white, cream or yellow body; the marks do not go round the belly.
A pointed red snout.
The belly is plain white or cream.

look.colour: Red, black and white or yellow
look.pattern: Black-edged red saddles over a pale body
look.head: Pointed, with a red snout

fact: Its marks stop at the sides, leaving a white belly: one quick way to tell it from coral snakes and kingsnakes.

name: Eastern Glossy Snake
habitat: Sandy prairie, grassland and desert scrub
range: The southern plains: Kansas, Colorado, Oklahoma, Texas and New Mexico; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, rodents and small snakes
ids: Pale tan or cream with brown, dark-edged blotches down the back: like a faded gophersnake.
Very smooth, shiny scales (gophersnakes have ridged ones).
A narrow head with a slightly overhanging snout, and a plain white belly.
fact: It burrows in sand by day and is mostly seen crossing roads on warm nights.

name: Western Glossy Snake
habitat: Desert flats, sandy scrub and grassland
range: California, Nevada, Utah and Arizona; into Mexico
diet: Lizards, rodents and small snakes
ids: Pale cream, buff or grey with brown dark-edged blotches.
Very smooth, glossy scales and a plain belly.
A narrow head with an overhanging snout and large eyes.
fact: The western glossy snakes were separated from the eastern ones in 2021.

name: Long-nosed Snake
habitat: Desert scrub, grassland and sandy or rocky flats
range: The south-west and southern plains: California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas; into Mexico
diet: Lizards and their eggs, and small rodents
ids: Black saddles and red patches on a cream body, with white or yellow specks inside the black and black specks in the red.
A long, pointed snout that juts past the lower jaw.
Smooth scales; the belly is plain cream.

look.pattern: Speckled black saddles and red patches
look.head: Long and pointed

fact: When handled it may bleed from its vent and smear a foul musk to discourage predators.

name: Eastern Hog-nosed Snake
habitat: Sandy woods, fields, beaches, dunes and open pine forest
range: Eastern North America, from southern Ontario and New England to Florida, west to Minnesota, Kansas and Texas
diet: Toads, frogs and salamanders
ids: A thick-bodied snake with an upturned, shovel-like snout.
Very variable colour: yellow, tan, grey, olive, orange or all black, usually with dark blotches.
When threatened it flattens its neck like a cobra, hisses loudly, and then rolls over and plays dead with its mouth open.
Keeled scales; the underside of the tail is paler than the belly.

look.colour: Yellow, tan, grey, orange or black
look.head: Upturned, shovel-like snout

fact: Its rear teeth and mild saliva help it deal with toads; it almost never bites people, preferring to play dead.

name: Plains Hog-nosed Snake
habitat: Sandy and gravelly prairie, grassland and river floodplains
range: The Great Plains, from Alberta and Saskatchewan to Texas and New Mexico
diet: Toads, frogs, lizards, mice and reptile eggs
ids: A stout snake with a sharply upturned, pointed snout.
Tan or grey with darker brown blotches down the back.
A black belly with yellow or white patches.
Flattens its neck, hisses and plays dead when threatened.

look.colour: Tan or grey with brown blotches
look.head: Sharply upturned snout

fact: It uses its snout like a shovel to dig up toads and buried turtle eggs.

name: Mexican Hog-nosed Snake
habitat: Desert grassland, sandy flats and thornscrub
range: South and west Texas, southern New Mexico and south-eastern Arizona; into Mexico
diet: Toads, lizards and reptile eggs
ids: A stout snake with an upturned snout, tan with brown blotches.
Mostly black belly.
Told apart from the Plains Hog-nosed Snake mainly by where it lives.

look.colour: Tan or grey with brown blotches
look.head: Upturned snout

fact: Like other hognoses, it puts on a dramatic death act, even smelling of decay.

name: Southern Hog-nosed Snake
habitat: Sandhills, longleaf pine and scrub on deep sand
range: The south-eastern coastal plain: the Carolinas, Georgia, Florida and Alabama
diet: Toads and frogs
ids: The smallest hognose, with a very sharply upturned snout.
Grey, tan or reddish with dark blotches.
A plain pale belly, unlike the Eastern Hog-nosed Snake's.

look.colour: Grey, tan or reddish with dark blotches
look.head: Sharply upturned

fact: It has disappeared from much of its range and is now a rare snake of the sandhills.
